## 1.Guidelines on customs valuation

### a. Customs valuation for imported standalone application software (not attached to machinery or equipment)

The customs value is determined based on the actual price paid or payable for the carrier medium, excluding the value of the application software if, on the commercial invoice, the software value is separated from the value of the carrier medium. [...] If the price of software and the price of intermediaries can be separated: The customs value is the transaction value of imported machinery and equipment and control and operation software, excluding the value of intermediaries.

 If the price of the software and the price of the intermediary cannot be separated: The customs value is the transaction value of imported machinery and equipment and control and operation software, including the value of the intermediary. [...] ### b. Customs value when importing control and operation software

If the imported goods are machinery/equipment accompanied by control or operating software:  

 The customs value is the transaction value of the machinery/equipment together with the imported control or operating software.

results.title: Customs Valuation [Royalties] in Contract Manufacturing – Key Takeaways A recent India CESTAT ruling (Customs Appeal No. 40085/2024) provides important clarity on when royalties paid by a beneficial… | Douglas Mackay
results.content: Customs Valuation [Royalties] in Contract Manufacturing – Key Takeaways A recent India CESTAT ruling (Customs Appeal No. 40085/2024) provides important clarity on when royalties paid by a beneficial owner become dutiable, even if the importer of record is a contract manufacturer. What happened? Xiaomi India paid royalties/licence fees to Qualcomm and Beijing Xiaomi for technology embedded in imported components and finished goods. While many goods were manufactured by Indian contract [...] by Indian contract manufacturers, Xiaomi China controlled the import of components and the manufacturers could only sell their output to Xiaomi India. Revenue argued—and CESTAT agreed—that: The IP was embedded in the imported goods. Non-payment of royalties would halt imports entirely. Royalties were therefore a condition of sale and must be included in the customs assessable value. Xiaomi India, though not the importer of record, acted as the beneficial owner and was liable for valuation [...] for valuation impacts. Why it matters: Royalty payments linked to the right to import can trigger customs duty—even if paid by a party other than the importer. Beneficial ownership extends beyond legal title to include control, benefit, and contractual influence. Contract manufacturing and IP licensing structures must be carefully reviewed for customs implications. results.title: Mezan | What is Customs Valuation?
results.content:
Title: Mezan | What is Customs Valuation?
Customs Valuation refers to the systematic process of determining the dutiable value of imported goods for calculating customs duties, taxes, and fees. This valuation establishes the monetary worth of goods at the time and place of importation, serving as the foundation for assessing applicable customs charges. The process follows internationally recognized methods primarily based on the actual transaction value of goods. • **Transaction Value Method**: The primary valuation approach using the actual price paid or payable for goods, including all costs up to the port of importation • **Alternative Valuation Methods**: Secondary methods including identical goods value, similar goods value, deductive value, computed value, and fallback method when transaction value cannot be determined • **Adjustments and Additions**: Inclusion of costs such as packaging, assists provided by buyer, royalties, and proceeds from subsequent sales that affect the goods' value • **Documentation Requirements**: Comprehensive records including commercial invoices, contracts, payment evidence, and supporting documentation to substantiate declared values. The Kingdom applies the transaction value method as the primary basis for valuation, requiring importers to declare the actual price paid for goods including freight, insurance, and other charges up to the first port of entry. Businesses must maintain detailed records of all import transactions for a minimum of five years, including original commercial invoices, purchase contracts, payment confirmations, and shipping documents. Companies engaged in related-party transactions must provide additional documentation demonstrating that the transaction value reflects arm's length commercial terms. **Value Determination Complexity**: Businesses often struggle with correctly identifying all components that should be included in customs value, particularly regarding indirect costs, royalties, and subsequent sale proceeds. **Implement Robust Documentation Systems**: Maintain comprehensive records of all cost components and pricing decisions, ensuring documentation clearly supports declared values and can withstand customs scrutiny. **Regular Compliance Reviews**: Conduct periodic internal audits of valuation practices and seek professional guidance to ensure ongoing compliance with evolving customs regulations and WTO principles. Cloud accounting platforms like Mezan provide comprehensive financial analysis tools that help streamline customs valuation processes and efficiently manage financial data, enabling businesses to maintain accurate records and ensure regulatory compliance. For expert guidance on Customs Valuation methods and compliance, consider consulting with qualified tax and business advisors.

results.content:
Title: Customs valuation Archives - International Trade and Customs Blog
The opinion concludes that the entire royalty has been reinstated in the value of the input, since the conditions of Article 8.1.c of the Customs Valuation Agreement (i.e., the relationship of the royalty with the input and its payment as a condition of the sale export of the input) are met. **The Court of Justice of the European Union (hereinafter “CJEU”), in a judgment dated November 19, 2020 (case C 775/19, 5th Avenue), interpreted the conditions for reintegrating, in the customs value of imported goods, royalties paid by a buyer in exchange for the right to exclusively distribute these goods within the territory of the European union.**. In **situations where intangible assets, provided in return of a payment of royalties, are identified as production factors, assessment of their dutiability will be made following article 71-1-b UCC rather than article 71-1-c**, whose conditions make it more difficult for administrations to reintegrate in customs value. The Court of Justice of the European Union (“**ECJ**“), in a judgment of 10 September 2020 (BMW Bayerische Motorenwerke AG, case C509/19), interpreted Article 71-1-b of the Union Customs Code (“**UCC**“) relating to adjustments made to the transaction value. Referred for a preliminary ruling, the Court of Justice of the European Union interpreted, in a judgment of 9 July 2020, *Direktor na Teritorialna direktsiya Yugozapadna Agentsiya “Mitnitsi”*, case C-76/19, Article 32-1-c of regulation (EEC) 2913/92 establishing the Community customs code (“CCC”), relating to the conditions for reintegrating royalties and license fees into the customs value of imported goods. Will this give hope to operators who see, in the drafting of the UCC customs valuation rules, a mechanism implying automatic integration of royalties into the value of imported goods? The two issues submitted by a member to the TCCV in this Advisory Opinion 23.1 were whether a highly discounted price of goods purchased could be accepted as the basis for customs valuation under Article 1 and whether the discounted price could be used to determine the transaction value of identical or similar goods for which there is no transaction value.

results.content:
Title: Customs Valuation - New Update from the WCO on Royalties and Licence Fees - Global Import Blog
### *Tariffs. # Customs Valuation – New Update from the WCO on Royalties and Licence Fees. By Yassine El Bojaddaini (Netherlands)") and Johanna Asplund (UK)") 1 Min Read. Share on Facebook   Share on Twitter   Email. During the latest session of the Technical Committee on Customs Valuation (“TCCV”), the TCCV adopted Advisory Opinion 4.19, a new instrument on royalties and licence fees under Article 8.1(c) of the Customs Valuation Agreement (“CVA”). The new Opinion advises on how a single royalty paid for the right to use or incorporate a patented imported input in the production of a finished product in the country of importation and how the use of a trademark on the finished product is to be treated for customs valuation purposes. The full text of the opinion is not yet available, since it still has to be approved by the WCO Counsel. The Opinion will also need to be reported to the WTO Committee on Customs Valuation before it will be fully published in the WCO Customs Valuation Compendium. Note that – once published – the Opinion is not legally binding on customs administrations. Advisory Opinions, however, serve as useful guidance for the interpretation of the CVA. Furthermore, Advisory Opinions and other instruments adopted by the TCCV may enhance the uniform application of the CVA. results.title: Preloaded Software Must Be Included in Customs Valuation of Imported Navigation Devices: CESTAT [Read Order]
results.content:
Title: Preloaded Software Must Be Included in Customs Valuation of Imported Navigation Devices: CESTAT [Read Order]
# Preloaded Software Must Be Included in Customs Valuation of Imported Navigation Devices: CESTAT [Read Order]. ## CESTAT held that preloaded software forms part of the imported navigation devices’ value and is liable to customs duty. ![Preloaded Software Must Be Included in Customs Valuation of Imported Navigation Devices: CESTAT [Read Order]](https://images.taxscan.in/h-upload/2025/09/08/2084636-preloaded-software-customs-valuation-imported-navigation-devices-taxscan.webp "Preloaded Software Must Be Included in Customs Valuation of Imported Navigation Devices: CESTAT [Read Order]"). The Bangalore Bench of the Customs, Excise, and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) ruled that the value of preloaded software must be included in the customs valuation of imported navigation devices.Lakshmi Access Communications Systems Pvt. Ltd., the appellant, imported 20,150 GPS navigation devices and 20,000 paper software licences under separate bills of entry in April 2010. The Bangalore Bench of the Customs, Excise, and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal (CESTAT) ruled that the value of preloaded software must be included in the customs valuation of imported navigation devices. Lakshmi Access Communications Systems Pvt. Ltd., the appellant, imported 20,150 GPS navigation devices and 20,000 paper software licences under separate bills of entry in April 2010. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI) investigated the imports, alleging undervaluation by splitting hardware and software invoices and claiming exemption for the software. The appellant’s counsel argued that paper licences for software were exempt from basic customs duty under Notification No. 21/2002-Cus and that their value could not be added to hardware. The appellant’s counsel relied on Supreme Court rulings in PSI Data Systems and Acer India to submit that software had an independent identity and its value was not includable in the hardware. The revenue counsel countered that the software was already etched and preloaded into the navigation devices and licence keys were imprinted on the hardware. The two-member bench comprising Dr. D.M. Misra (Judicial Member) and Pullela Nageswara Rao (Technical Member) observed that the software was preloaded into the navigation devices and the licence keys were already imprinted, making the software an integral part of the hardware. The tribunal held that the commissioner was right in enhancing the value by including the software component, confirming the duty demand, interest, and confiscation.
